newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico cenbank denies pump-priming economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico cenbank denies pump-priming economy.

text.p: Mexico's central bank firmly denied it was pumping up the economy ahead of key elections this year after speculation it was succumbing to political pressure swirled around financial markets on Wednesday.

Although independent of the government since early 1994, the Bank of Mexico has been accused by market investors and opposition politicians of injecting more money into the financial system to spur the economy in past election years.
Economists said on Wednesday they were concerned money supply levels exceeding the bank's own forecasts meant the bank has been acting to give the economy a pre-election fillip.
"We reject that accusation definitely," a central bank spokesman told Reuters.
"The phenomenon we are witnessing -- the difference between projections and the actual figure -- is demand-determined," he added. "The demand is exogenous to the actions of the central bank."

Economists have been concerned for some weeks about monetary base numbers -- a measure of notes and coins in circulation -- that show the central bank overshooting its own daily estimates in supplying markets hungry for cash.
Worries have been particularly strong since public holidays in early May when levels climbed to meet a normal rise in demand but subsequently failed to come down.
Economists from New York to London have been anxious for an official explanation of the rise.

"Especially in the last three weeks the deviation from the bank's own targets has been high...this is not a trivial statistical miss," independent Mexico City economist Jonathan Heath said earlier on Wednesday.

Mexico's monetary base has been pushing at the upper limit of the bank's stated 2.6 percent level of standard deviation since Easter, surpassing it to the tune of 6.6 percent on average over the past five to six days, analysts said.
The development came as campaigns heated up for the July 1997 mid-term congressional and local elections.

"The cynical view is that the Bank of Mexico is pumping money supply before the elections to make sure the economy is doing well, but the bank may argue that there is a normal increase in demand for money which, if it is not satisfied, would lead to high interest rates and slow economic activity," Heath said.

"The problem is that both may be right -- there may be increased demand but the bank is not doing anything to moderate it," he said, adding even a symbolic signal that it was unhappy with the increased demand would do much to quell suspicions.
The central bank spokesman, however, said demand was rising naturally due to a pick-up in economic activity.

"Economic activity and unemployment have come in stronger than expected, and at the same time inflation has come down faster than expected, and this has produced a stronger demand for means of payment," he said.
Ann Ginsburg at Valores Finamex in New York said there was no evidence to suggest the central bank was doing anything untoward.

"I don't think the central bank is being irresponsible," she said. "People always get suspicious before elections but if they were supplying more than the economy needed you would see it in the peso, in interest rates, in inflation and in the level of reserves."
Those areas of the economy are all in good shape, she said..

Mexico's financial markets were firm at midsession on Wednesday despite the controversy. Dealers said the peso and stocks were strong following the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision not to raise U.S. interest rates.
